Keywords: Street, Yarn, Roses

outputs.L1:
**Street Yarn**

Roses, caged in windows, heighten  
Your faint blooms today;  
Silks and sheeny satins, brighten—  
He has passed this way!

Could ye keep his fleeting presence,  
Gone beyond recall,  
But a little of his essence,  
I would have you all.

Arabesque, so quaint and shady,  
That mightst catch his eye  
To adorn a stately lady  
Ere her hour went by,

Canst assure me that his glancing  
Rested on thy fold?  
Did that set your purples dancing,  
Wake the sleepy gold?

Ye neglected apple-venders,  
Mouldering in the street,  
Did he curse between your tenders,  
Spurning with his feet?

Then must I an alms deliver  
For his graceless pride;  
Could I buy his sins forever,  
I’d not be denied—

Paying patiently his ransom,  
Never conscience-pricked;  
Cheating Justice of her handsome,  
Heartless derelict.

Did he view thee, ancient steeple,  
With thy weird clock-face,  
Frowning down on sinful people  
Passing out of grace?

Nay, respond not to my question  
With thy prate of time:  
Things to which my soul must hasten  
Lie beyond thy chime.

With no circumstance to screen us,  
We must meet again:  
I shall bid God judge between us,  
Answering, “Amen.”
outputs.L2:
### Street Tale

Roses trapped behind shopfront glass,  
Let your pale blossoms glow more strongly today;  
Silks and gleaming satins, shine—  
He once walked past this place.

If you could preserve his vanished presence,  
Though he has gone beyond retrieval,  
I would ask each of you to hold  
Even the smallest trace of him.

Strange, shadowed arabesque,  
Perhaps you caught his attention  
Before adorning some noblewoman  
Whose final hour had not yet come.

Can you promise that his gaze  
Paused upon your folds?  
Did it stir your purple colors  
And rouse the drowsing gold?

You forgotten sellers of apples,  
Decaying there along the street,  
Did he curse among your offerings  
And kick them aside?

If so, I must give charity  
To atone for his shameless arrogance.  
If I could purchase pardon for all his sins,  
No price would make me refuse.

I would steadily pay for his release,  
Never troubled by conscience,  
And cheat Justice of the splendid  
Yet unfeeling outcast she claims.

Old steeple, did he look at you  
And your uncanny clock face  
Scowling upon sinful people  
As they slipped away from grace?

No—do not answer me  
With your endless talk of passing time.  
The things toward which my spirit must hurry  
Exist beyond the reach of your bells.

With no ceremony or circumstance to shield us,  
He and I must meet once more.  
I will ask God to decide between us,  
And I will answer, “Amen.”
outputs.L3:
The speaker searches the street for any trace of the man who has passed by. She looks closely at the flowers, fabrics, vendors, and familiar landmarks, hoping that something in the scene might retain a sign of his presence. Even the smallest connection matters to her: she longs to preserve an object he may have seen, noticed, or touched, as though it could keep a fragment of that fleeting moment alive.

Her love is marked by profound, almost self-sacrificing devotion. She is willing to accept the burden of his cruelty, pride, and sins, paying their price without hesitation if doing so might bind her to him. At the same time, she refuses to submit to the ancient steeple’s reminder that earthly time passes and all human experiences must end. She believes that her soul is destined for concerns beyond temporal life and that death cannot make their separation final.

The poem closes with her unwavering conviction that they will meet again in the presence of God. In that ultimate encounter, earthly uncertainty will give way to divine judgment, and God will decide between them, revealing the truth of their relationship and the meaning of her devotion.
outputs.L4:
She follows the road he once took, searching the city for some trace of him. At every turning, ordinary sights seem charged with his absence: flowers tremble in the market stalls, bright fabrics hang from shopfronts, vendors call across the crowded street, and a steeple rises above the roofs. She questions each of them as though they might have caught and kept something of him—a glance, a word, the touch of his passing—but none can answer her. The street remains vivid and alive, while the man she seeks has vanished beyond its reach.

She tries to hold him through memory, yet memory proves too fragile. Love cannot restore him, sorrow cannot cleanse what lay between them, and no offering or ransom can purchase his return. Whatever guilt, injury, or unfinished longing bound them together in life must remain unresolved on earth. Her devotion is powerless against death, and even her grief cannot redeem him.

Still, she believes their separation is not eternal. She imagines a final meeting before God, where neither can hide behind silence, distance, or the distortions of memory. There, their troubled bond will be fully revealed and judged. What she cannot understand or settle now will at last receive its answer—not from the streets that remember nothing, nor from love that could not save him, but from divine justice.
outputs.L5:
At the end of the street stood a house wrapped in silence. Wild roses climbed its iron gate, blooming red against the gray stone.

Every morning, an old woman sat by the window with a basket of yarn at her feet. She knitted scarves in colors bright enough to challenge the weather—gold for sunlight, blue for hope, green for spring.

One cold evening, she tied the scarves along the street, winding them around lampposts and bare trees. By dawn, the neighborhood had become a soft, colorful path leading to her gate.

There, beneath the roses, a small sign read:

**Take what you need. Leave a little warmth behind.**

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical poem in an early-20th-century style about a woman walking through city streets haunted by the memory of a sinful, absent lover.
counterfactuals.output:
At dusk she walks where lamps awake  
Like pale confessions in the rain,  
And every window seems to shake  
With some remembered, scarlet stain.  

The pavements shine; the carriages pass;  
A bell mourns over roof and spire.  
His shadow, dark in every glass,  
Still wears the rose she gave desire.  

O faithless mouth, O vanished breath,  
That taught her innocence to burn—  
Though he has gone beyond her path,  
The midnight corners watch his return.  

She hears his laughter down the square,  
Where fallen blossoms choke the stone;  
She turns—there is but empty air,  
A shuttered house, a moon gone wan.  

Yet through the city’s ashen maze  
She bears his sin beneath her breast,  
A secret flame from other days  
No prayer can quiet into rest.  

And when the dawn, in widow’s gray,  
Unseals the roofs above the street,  
She walks alone into the day—  
His ghost still keeping step with her feet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a rhyming dramatic monologue that addresses shop-window flowers, luxurious fabrics, apple vendors, and an ancient clock tower before ending with an appeal to God’s judgment.
counterfactuals.output:
O flowers behind glass, too flawless to fade,  
You bloom where the debts of the desperate are paid;  
Your petals are proud in their glittering shrine—  
Have you never felt frost, as this poor heart of mine?

O velvets and satins, in violet and gold,  
You ripple like rivers no beggar may hold;  
You clothe the pale mannequins, stately and tall,  
While hunger goes shivering under your wall.

O vendors of apples, whose barrows glow red,  
You cry out your wares where the weary are fed;  
One fruit in my palm seems an orchard restored—  
Yet even sweet plenty belongs to some lord.

O tower, old keeper of iron-tongued Time,  
You toll every sorrow and silence each crime;  
Your hands circle onward, indifferent and grim,  
While kings turn to shadows and bright eyes grow dim.

And I, who have wandered through splendor and fraud,  
Now lift my last plea past the rooftops to God:  
When rich cloth is ashes and proud towers fall,  
Judge not by our fortunes—have mercy on all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a melancholic urban poem titled “Street Yarn,” using archaic diction, alternating rhymes, and themes of love, guilt, ransom, and divine justice.
counterfactuals.output:
# Street Yarn

Beneath yon lamps that bled upon the rain,  
I sought thy face where midnight tramcars moan;  
The gutters sang our old, forbidden pain,  
And every shutter judged me, stone by stone.  

Thy love was gold I stole from Heaven’s toll,  
Then bartered ’neath the market’s faithless light;  
Now guilt, that sable watchman, haunts my soul,  
And chalks my trespass on the walls each night.  

They haled thee where the iron bridges loom,  
And named thy ransom ere the cock should cry;  
I brought but grief unto that shuttered room—  
The sirens wailed, and thou wert left to die.  

“Have mercy, Lord,” quoth I, “behold my scar;  
I sinned for love—let love my sin efface.”  
But Justice gazed from each unpitying star,  
And would not turn the scales for my disgrace.  

Now through the lanes I wander, old and blind,  
Whilst neon saints burn blue without a name;  
No coin may buy thee from the earth unkind,  
Nor tears redeem me from celestial flame.  

Thus spins the street its yarn, a blood-dark thread,  
From tavern door to tenement above:  
That God collects the debts of quick and dead—  
And guilt outlives the ransom paid for love.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you create a vintage Gothic poem in which the speaker searches for traces of a departed man among street stalls and storefronts, insisting that they will meet again before God?
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Black Arcade**

At dawn I haunt the market-square,  
Where awnings drip with rain,  
And search the merchants’ tarnished wares  
For some lost sign again:  
Your glove among the mourning lace,  
Your shadow on the pane.  

I question every flower-girl  
Who binds her ashen rose;  
I start when through the shuttered shops  
A coat like midnight goes.  
Yet only bells beneath the fog  
Reply with iron throes.  

Your likeness pales in silver frames,  
Your step haunts every door;  
The bookstall keeps the psalms you loved,  
The wine-shop stains the floor.  
But dust has sealed your quiet mouth,  
And you return no more.  

Still, death is but a narrow street  
Where lamps burn dim and far;  
Beyond its last and darkest stall  
The soul stands where you are.  
No earthly lock, no marble vault,  
Can bar that judgment-star.  

So let the rain erase your tracks,  
Let blackened windows nod—  
I shall not seek forever here  
Through market-mire and clod.  
We two shall meet, and speak again,  
Before the throne of God.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem reminiscent of Edna St. Vincent Millay or Elinor Wylie, with short quatrains, vivid silks and roses, personified city objects, and a bitter final “Amen.”
counterfactuals.output:
The moon wears silver watered silk  
Above the shuttered square;  
The lamp-post, pale and thin with grief,  
Keeps watch for no one there.  

Red roses bruise the window glass,  
Their petals dark as wine;  
The chimneys bow like widowers  
Before a faithless shrine.  

Along the curb the gutters hiss  
Of vows the rain betrayed;  
The clock-tower bites its brazen tongue,  
Ashamed of what it said.  

I wore your scarlet promises  
As queens wear cloth of gold;  
Now every thread has learned the frost,  
And every rose the cold.  

Let bells put on their blackest gloves,  
Let dawn deny the day;  
Love was a beggar dressed in silk  
Who stole my heart away.  

So bless the streets that watched him go,  
The stones that knew him when—  
And bless the lie I called my life.  
Amen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
